chapter.title: Heaps and graphs
chapter.summary: Priority queues for always-the-best-next-item problems, and graphs for everything that is connected.

lessons.title: Heaps and priority queues
lessons.summary: How a binary heap keeps the smallest item on top, and the top-K and merge patterns it unlocks.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## The problem

You keep receiving items and repeatedly need the **smallest** (or largest) one: the next task by priority, the closest point, the k-th largest score. Sorting after every insert costs `O(n log n)` each time. A **heap** gives you the minimum in `O(1)` and supports insert and remove-min in `O(log n)`.

A **priority queue** is the abstract idea ("remove the highest-priority item"); a **binary heap** is the standard way to build one.

## The shape: a complete binary tree stored in an array

A **min-heap** is a binary tree where every parent is **less than or equal to** its children. So the **minimum is always at the root**. (A max-heap is the reverse.) Siblings have no order between them.

The tree is **complete** (every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right), so it fits in a plain array with no pointers:

- parent of `i`: `(i - 1) / 2` (integer division)
- left child: `2i + 1`
- right child: `2i + 2`

```
        1            array: [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]
      /   \
     3     2
    / \   /
   7   4 5
```

## Two core operations

**Insert (push):** append at the end, then **sift up**: while the new item is smaller than its parent, swap them. At most `log n` swaps because the height is `log n`.

**Remove min (pop):** take the root. Move the **last** item to the root, then **sift down**: swap with the smaller child while it is bigger than that child. At most `log n` swaps.

**Build a heap from n items:** inserting one by one is `O(n log n)`, but **heapify** (sift down from the last parent back to the root) is **O(n)**.

## What heaps cannot do

A heap is **not sorted** and **not searchable**: finding an arbitrary value is `O(n)`. Use it only when you need repeated access to the extreme.

## Language support

- Python `heapq` (min-heap on a list; for a max-heap push negated values).
- Java `PriorityQueue` (min-heap by default; pass a comparator for max).
- C++ `priority_queue` is a **max**-heap by default; use `greater<int>` for min.
- JavaScript has **no built-in heap**; write a small class (shown below) or use a library.

## The patterns

### 1. Top-K largest: keep a **min-heap of size k**

Iterate through the data. Push each item; if the heap grows past `k`, pop the smallest. At the end the heap holds the k largest and the **root is the k-th largest**. Time `O(n log k)`, space `O(k)`. This beats sorting (`O(n log n)`) when `k` is small and works on streams that don't fit in memory.

(Why a *min*-heap for the *largest*? The root is the weakest of the current top k, the first to be evicted.)

### 2. Merge k sorted lists

Put the head of each list in a min-heap. Pop the smallest, append to the result, push that list's next element. `O(N log k)` for `N` total items.

### 3. Running median: two heaps

A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size. The median sits at the top(s). Insert in `O(log n)`, median in `O(1)`.

### 4. Scheduling and simulation

Task scheduler, meeting rooms (heap of end times), Dijkstra's shortest path (heap of frontier distances).

## Pitfalls

- Choosing the wrong heap type for top-K (use min-heap of size k for largest).
- Forgetting that C++ `priority_queue` is a max-heap.
- Comparator mistakes with tuples; store `(priority, item)`.
- Expecting iteration over a heap to be sorted.

diagrams.title: Min-heap: every parent is at most its children

code.source:
import heapq

# K-th largest: min-heap of size k. O(n log k) time, O(k) space
def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return heap[0]

# Merge k sorted lists: O(N log k)
def merge_k_sorted(lists):
    heap = [(l[0], i, 0) for i, l in enumerate(lists) if l]
    heapq.heapify(heap)                 # O(k)
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(val)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

# Max-heap trick: push negated values
max_heap = []
heapq.heappush(max_heap, -5)
largest = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)

keyPoints: A binary heap keeps the extreme value at the root of a complete tree stored in an array.
Push and pop are O(log n) via sift up and sift down; peek is O(1); heapify builds in O(n).
For the k largest, keep a MIN-heap of size k; the root is the k-th largest.
A heap is not sorted and not searchable; use it only for repeated min or max access.
JavaScript has no built-in heap, and C++ priority_queue is a max-heap by default.

check.q: To find the k largest numbers in a stream, which structure is best?
check.why: The min-heap root is the smallest of the current top k, so it is the one to evict when a bigger item arrives.

check.q: What is the index of the left child of the node at index i in an array heap?
check.why: With 0-based indexes, children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

check.q: Why is building a heap by heapify O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
options: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance
check.why: Half the nodes are leaves needing no work; the work summed over levels converges to O(n).

lessons.title: Graphs: BFS and DFS
lessons.summary: Modelling problems as nodes and edges, storing them, and exploring them breadth-first and depth-first, on grids and general graphs.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## What a graph is

A **graph** is a set of **vertices** (nodes) and **edges** (connections). Maps, social networks, web links, course prerequisites, game states and grids are all graphs. A tree is just a connected graph with no cycles.

- **Directed** edges go one way (follow, prerequisite); **undirected** go both.
- **Weighted** edges carry a cost (distance); **unweighted** do not.
- **Connected**: every node reachable from every other. A graph may have several **components**.
- **Cycle**: a path that returns to its start. A directed graph with no cycles is a **DAG**.

## How to store a graph

**Adjacency list** (use this almost always): for each node, a list of its neighbours. Space `O(V + E)`; iterating neighbours is fast.

```
0: [1, 2]
1: [0, 3]
2: [0]
3: [1]
```

**Adjacency matrix**: a `V × V` grid where `m[i][j] = 1` if an edge exists. Space `O(V²)`; edge lookup `O(1)`; only good for dense graphs.

**Grids** are implicit graphs: each cell is a node, neighbours are the 4 (or 8) adjacent cells; no list needed, just direction offsets.

## The key requirement: remember what you visited

Graphs can have cycles, so without a **visited set** you loop forever. Mark a node visited *when you first discover it*.

## BFS: breadth-first search

Explore **layer by layer** outward from the start using a **queue**: all nodes 1 step away, then 2 steps, and so on.

```
queue = [start]; visited = {start}
while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()
    for nb in neighbours(node):
        if nb not in visited:
            visited.add(nb); queue.append(nb)
```

**Superpower:** in an **unweighted** graph, BFS finds the **shortest path** (fewest edges) because it reaches every node by the smallest number of steps first. Use it for shortest path in a maze, minimum moves, word ladder, level-order traversal.

## DFS: depth-first search

Go as **deep** as possible down one path, then backtrack. Use recursion (the call stack) or an explicit **stack**.

```
dfs(node):
    visited.add(node)
    for nb in neighbours(node):
        if nb not in visited: dfs(nb)
```

Use it for: **connected components**, **flood fill / number of islands**, **cycle detection**, **topological sort**, path existence, exploring all possibilities (backtracking).

## BFS vs DFS

| | BFS | DFS |
|---|---|---|
| Data structure | queue | stack / recursion |
| Explores | layer by layer | one branch fully |
| Shortest path (unweighted) | **yes** | no |
| Memory | up to the widest layer | up to the deepest path |
| Natural for | distances, levels | components, cycles, ordering |

Both run in `O(V + E)` with an adjacency list.

## Worked example: number of islands

A grid of `1` (land) and `0` (water); count connected groups of land. Scan every cell; when you find an unvisited `1`, **increment the count and flood-fill** its whole island (DFS or BFS), marking cells visited (e.g. set to `0`). Each cell is entered once: `O(rows × cols)`.

## Cycle detection and topological sort (preview)

- **Undirected cycle**: DFS meets a visited node that is not its parent.
- **Directed cycle**: DFS meets a node that is on the *current recursion path*.
- **Topological order** (course schedule): repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0 (Kahn's algorithm, BFS-style). If you cannot take them all, there is a cycle.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the visited set (infinite loops) or marking visited too late (the same node enqueued many times).
- Recursion depth overflow on a huge DFS: use an explicit stack.
- Mutating the grid when you still need the original.
- Directed vs undirected: for undirected edges, add both directions.
- Disconnected graphs: loop over all nodes, not just node 0.

diagrams.title: BFS explores in layers; DFS dives down one branch
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  S["start"] --> A["layer 1: A"]
  S --> B["layer 1: B"]
  A --> C["layer 2: C"]
  A --> D["layer 2: D"]
  B --> E["layer 2: E"]

keyPoints: Store graphs as adjacency lists (O(V + E)); grids are implicit graphs with direction offsets.
Always keep a visited set, and mark nodes visited when first discovered.
BFS uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS uses a stack or recursion.
Both traversals are O(V + E); use DFS for components, cycles and ordering.
Loop over every node to handle disconnected graphs, and add both directions for undirected edges.

check.q: You need the fewest moves between two cells of an unweighted maze. Which algorithm?
check.why: BFS reaches every node by the minimum number of edges first, so the first time it reaches the goal is the shortest path.

check.q: What goes wrong if a graph traversal has no visited set?
options: It can loop forever on cycles and revisit nodes many times
check.why: Cycles let you walk the same nodes repeatedly; the visited set guarantees each node is processed once.

check.q: What is the time complexity of BFS on an adjacency list with V nodes and E edges?
check.why: Each node is dequeued once and each edge examined once (twice for undirected), giving O(V + E).
